newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey's Yilmaz begins tough coalition search.
newsitem.headline: Turkey's Yilmaz begins tough coalition search.

text.p: Prime minister-designate Mesut Yilmaz has started trying to build a secularist coalition to replace the Islamist-led government that locked horns with Turkey's powerful army leadership and lost.
Yilmaz scheduled a meeting of his conservative Motherland Party for Saturday in the first stage of what he said would be a short campaign to win support for an anti-Islamist alliance.
"In nine days, that is the second Monday from now, I will give the government list to the president," Yilmaz told a news conference after President Suleyman Demirel handed him the government mandate.

Yilmaz must patch together a coalition from among a host of squabbling leaders after this week's resignation by Necmettin Erbakan, modern Turkey's first Islamist leader, who was edged out of office by a hostile secularist establishment.
Yilmaz said he would meet party leaders, including his bitter personal rival Tansu Ciller, on Tuesday for talks on forming a coalition aimed at taking the country to spring elections.

His Motherland Party fields just 129 MPs in the 550-seat parliament. Two leftist parties have said they were prepared to back him, but he would still require substantial defections from Ciller's rival conservative True Path Party.
Erbakan, who said Yilmaz's selection was against democratic practice, quit on Wednesday after rumblings from the army that it was prepared to use force against his Islamist supporters.
"The president gave Yilmaz the responsibility to form a government that will defuse the current tension in the country," Demirel's office said in a statement.
Pro-Western Ciller, who served as Erbakan's deputy prime minister, was also in the running for the top job. She has the backing of 282 deputies, at least on paper.

But Demirel, a veteran of political in-fighting, rejected a plan for a Ciller-led coalition and instead followed Turkish tradition by choosing Yilmaz as leader of the second-biggest faction in parliament after Erbakan himself.

Ciller, who became Turkey's first woman prime minister in 1993, drew the wrath of the secularist establishment for going into coalition with the Erbakan's Islam-based Welfare Party last year after pledging not to do so.
She described Yilmaz's appointment, announced at the president's Cankaya palace, as akin to a military coup.
"We have come face to face with a Cankaya coup. This is disgraceful for democracy," Ciller told the TGRT television channel.

The powerful secularist military, which has staged three coups since 1960, played a key role in Erbakan's downfall with demands for a crackdown on the alleged rising profile of Islamists under his rule.
